objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the pilot in command's authority under 91.3, list what 91.103 requires you to know before a flight, work out the minimum fuel for day VFR, night VFR and IFR under 91.151 and 91.167, and get a complete preflight briefing.
why: Fuel-related accidents are one of the top four causes of fatal general aviation accidents, and they usually start with a planning shortcut on the ground. Knowing exactly what the rules require, and where they stop, lets you plan well above the minimum.

prereading.what: PIC responsibility and authority, and the preflight action rule, word for word.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.3 and 91.103

prereading.what: VFR and IFR fuel requirements and the alternate (1-2-3) test.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.151, 91.167, 91.169(b)

prereading.printed: AC 91-92, paras 6 to 8 and Appendixes A and B
prereading.what: Self-briefing, briefing types and checklists, do's and don'ts, and a sample preflight checklist.
prereading.label: AC 91-92, paras 6 to 8 and Appendixes A and B

prereading.what: Preflight briefing: standard, abbreviated, outlook and inflight briefings and what each contains.
prereading.label: AIM 7-1-5

prereading.what: Preflight preparation: Flight Service contacts, NOTAMs you must ask for, and what to tell the briefer.
prereading.label: AIM 5-1-1

prereading.what: Runway slope and surface, takeoff, cruise and landing charts with worked samples.

warmup: Think first: you are about to fly 20 minutes to a nearby airport for breakfast, a trip you have made dozens of times. What does the regulation say you must know before you go, and what would you actually check?

key_terms.def: The person with final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the flight (14 CFR 1.1).
Becoming familiar with all available information about a flight before you begin it (14 CFR 91.103).
From the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
Your first planned stop. The VFR fuel reserve is counted from there.
The speed (and fuel burn) at which the 30 or 45 minute reserves are figured.
Where you will go if you can't land at your destination. IFR fuel must cover it unless the 1-2-3 test is met.
Destination has an instrument approach, and from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA: ceiling at least 2,000 ft and visibility at least 3 SM. No alternate fuel needed.
The complete briefing, for when you have had no earlier briefing or online information.
Updates an earlier briefing or gives one or two specific items.
For a departure 6 or more hours away. Planning only.
Your own review of weather and aeronautical information using online and automated sources. May be regulatory compliant.
Advisory to ATC that you can't accept undue delay. Not an emergency and no priority.

chunks.title: The PIC: final authority and full responsibility

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.3(a): The pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

body.p: 14 CFR 1.1 adds who that is: the person who has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the flight, was designated as PIC before or during the flight, and holds the right category, class and type rating, if needed [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

head: Situation
Rule
What it says
rows: In-flight emergency that needs immediate action
You may deviate from any Part 91 rule as far as needed to meet that emergency [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]
You deviated from a rule under 91.3(b)
Send a written report to the FAA, but only on the Administrator's request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]]
You deviate from an ATC clearance or instruction in an emergency
Tell ATC about the deviation as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]
ATC gives you priority in an emergency (no rule broken)
Detailed report within 48 hours to the facility manager, if ATC requests it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]]

callout.text: Common mistake: thinking every emergency deviation needs a written report. Under 91.3(c) you send one only if the Administrator asks, and under 91.123(d) only if ATC asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

body.p: The AIM says the same thing: the PIC is the final authority as to the safe operation of the aircraft. Pilot and controller duties overlap on purpose, so one can catch the other's misses [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]].

Authority and responsibility come together. You make the go or no-go call and you own the result. What is legal under the rules and what is safe for you today are not always the same [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

check.q: In an emergency you leave your assigned altitude without a clearance, and ATC gives you priority. What must you do about it?
check.a: Tell ATC about the deviation as soon as possible. A detailed report within 48 hours is due only if ATC asks [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

chunks.title: 91.103: what you must know before every flight

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.103: Each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. This information must include ... [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]

head: Paragraph
Applies to
Must include
rows: A flight under IFR, or a flight not in the vicinity of an airport
Weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed, and any known traffic delays ATC has advised you of [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]
Runway lengths at airports of intended use, plus takeoff and landing distance information [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]
Aircraft that must have an approved flight manual with takeoff and landing data
The takeoff and landing distance data in that manual [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]
Other reliable performance information for the expected airport elevation, runway slope, gross weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]

body.p: The list is the minimum. The opening sentence still asks for all available information about the flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]. AC 91-92 says to review all appropriate sources, including Chart Supplements, the AIM and NOTAMs, and calls preflight action a rehearsal of the whole flight with contingencies added [[37:6|AC 91-92 7.1]] [[37:7|AC 91-92 7.1]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "I'm only staying in the pattern, so 91.103 doesn't apply." Paragraph (b), runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data, applies to any flight, including a local one [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Known ATC delays: paragraph (a) names the ones ATC has advised you of. You can also look ahead. AC 91-92 points to the Air Traffic Control System Command Center and FAA online tools for delays and flow control advisories [[37:12|AC 91-92 7.4.1.10]].

callout.text: Use a checklist so you don't miss an area [[37:7|AC 91-92 7.1]]. AC 91-92 Appendix B lists the briefing items plus IMSAFE, PAVE, personal minimums, fuel, alternates, traffic delays, takeoff and landing distances, performance items (elevation, runway slope and condition, weight and balance) and a RAIM check [[37:20|AC 91-92 App B]].

check.q: You will fly three takeoffs and landings in the pattern at your home field. Which 91.103 items are specifically required?
check.a: Runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data, under 91.103(b). The (a) list is named for IFR flights and flights away from the airport, but you must still know all available information about the flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

chunks.title: Runway lengths and takeoff and landing data

body.p: Runway length, surface and slope come from the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]] [[1:270|PHAK Figure 11-17]].

callout.text: Changed: the Airport/Facility Directory (A/FD) is now the Chart Supplement U.S. Older books and pilots may still say A/FD [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]] [[37:5|AC 91-92 5.1]].

body.p: Slope matters. A 3% gradient means the runway height changes 3 ft for every 100 ft of length. An upslope lengthens the takeoff roll but usually shortens the landing roll. A downslope does the opposite [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

PHAK sample from this chart: 2,400 lb, 3,000 ft pressure altitude, 30 °C gives a 1,325 ft ground roll and 2,480 ft to clear a 50 ft obstacle. With an 18-knot headwind, take off 20% (10% for each 9 knots): 1,060 ft and 1,984 ft [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]].

bullets: Read the conditions and notes first. They tell you what the numbers assume [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]].
Landing weight is not takeoff weight. Recompute it for the fuel you will burn [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]].
Interpolate between columns. 1,250 ft is halfway between sea level (1,075 ft) and 2,500 ft (1,135 ft), so 1,105 ft to clear 50 ft [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]].
Surface changes the numbers. On this landing table, a dry grass runway adds 20% of the total-to-clear-50-ft figure [[1:283|PHAK Figure 11-32]].

callout.text: Book numbers come from a new airplane flown by a professional test pilot [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. Takeoffs and landings get more hazardous as the calculated performance approaches the runway length available [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Unfactored flight manual landing distances may show maximum performance, not normal operations [[27:9|AC 91-79B 1.8.19]].

check.q: Your destination runway slopes down in your landing direction. Will the landing roll be longer or shorter than the level-runway chart number?
check.a: Longer. Landing on a downsloping runway increases landing distance [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.151(a): No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, (1) during the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or (2) at night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]].

head: Words in the rule
What it means for you
rows: It is a check you make before takeoff [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]
Use forecast winds and your groundspeed, not no-wind true airspeed [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]] [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]
The reserve counts from your first planned stop, not your final destination [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]
Figure the 30 or 45 minutes at your normal cruise fuel burn [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]
From the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]

callout.text: Common mistake: mixing up the two "nights". Night currency under 61.57(b) uses 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. The 45-minute fuel reserve uses the 1.1 definition, which starts at the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

body.p: Cruise tables often show endurance with no reserve. In this PHAK sample, 5,000 ft at 2,400 rpm burns 6.9 GPH, and 38 gallons gives 5.5 hours [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. For day VFR, the longest leg you may plan is 5.5 - 0.5 = 5.0 hours [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]], and less once you count taxi and climb.
Plan for startup, taxi and the higher burn in the climb, and add fuel for an adequate reserve as a safety measure [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

check.q: Night VFR, 1 hour 30 minutes to your first stop at 10 GPH. Ignoring taxi and climb, what is the least fuel you may begin with?

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.167(a): No person may operate a civil aircraft in IFR conditions unless it carries enough fuel (considering weather reports and forecasts and weather conditions) to (1) complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing; (2) except as provided in paragraph (b), fly from that airport to the alternate airport; and (3) fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]].

head: VFR airplane (91.151)
IFR (91.167)
rows: Beginning a flight under VFR conditions [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]
First point of intended landing [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]
First airport of intended landing, then the alternate if one is required [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]]

body.p: Paragraph (b) drops the alternate leg only when both are true: the first airport of intended landing has a standard (Part 97) or special instrument approach, and weather reports or forecasts show, for at least 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, a ceiling of at least 2,000 ft above the airport elevation and visibility of at least 3 SM [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]]. 91.169(b) uses the same test for listing an alternate on the IFR flight plan [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]].

callout.text: 1-2-3: 1 hour either side of the ETA, 2,000 ft ceiling, 3 SM visibility [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]].
Common mistake: counting the 45 minutes from the destination. When an alternate is required, the 45 minutes starts after you reach the alternate [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]].

body.p: Alternate weather minimums and approach choices are covered in the IFR Area (Area V). Here, know the fuel math.

check.q: IFR: 1 hour 10 minutes to destination, 35 minutes to the alternate, 12 GPH. Minimum fuel?

body.p: You don't have to call Flight Service. Pilots can receive a regulatory compliant briefing without contacting Flight Service [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1a]], and the FAA considers that a self-briefing may be compliant [[37:7|AC 91-92 7.1]].

callout.text: Changed: the PHAK still says the briefing should come from a Flight Service specialist [[1:315|PHAK 13-5]]. The current AIM and AC 91-92 encourage self-briefing with automated resources and treat Flight Service as a consultative resource [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5a]] [[37:6|AC 91-92 6.2]].

body.p: Flight Service: www.1800wxbrief.com or 1-800-WX-BRIEF (1-800-992-7433); in Alaska, 1-833-AK-BRIEF [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1a]]. If you call, self-brief first [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1a]], and tell the briefer what you already got from other sources [[33:323|AIM 5-1-1f]].

head: Briefing
When
What you get
rows: You are planning a flight and have no earlier briefing or online information [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]]
The complete, detailed picture. Within 6 hours of flight [[37:8|AC 91-92 Table 1]]
To update an earlier briefing, supplement other data, or get one or two items [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5c]]
What you don't have yet and changes since. Say when and where you got the earlier information [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5c]]
Departure is 6 or more hours away [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5d]]
Forecasts for planning only. Get a standard or abbreviated briefing before you leave [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5d]]

body.p: Give the briefer, or your app, the background [[33:323|AIM 5-1-1e]]:

bullets: Type of flight: VFR or IFR
Aircraft number or pilot's name, and aircraft type
Departure airport, route and destination
Altitude(s)
ETD and ETE

callout.text: Get a standard briefing as close to departure as you can. Get an abbreviated one just before takeoff if the standard is 1 hour or more old or the weather is questionable [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

check.q: At 0600 you check weather for a 1500 departure. Which briefing type fits, and what do you do before takeoff?
check.a: An outlook briefing (6 or more hours out). Get a standard or abbreviated briefing before you depart [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5d]].

head: Element
Key point
rows: Weather or aeronautical items that might make you change or cancel: hazardous weather, airport closures, ATC delays [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]]
Advisory only. The final decision is the pilot's [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]]
Type, location and movement of weather systems and air masses [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]]
Left out if departure is more than 2 hours away, unless you ask [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]]
In order: departure and climbout, en route, descent [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]]
For your ETA, with significant changes from 1 hour before to 1 hour after [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]]
In knots and degrees true; temperatures on request [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]]
NOTAM (D)s for the flight, SUA NOTAMs for restricted areas, aerial refueling and NVG, plus P-40, P-49, P-56 and the DC SFRA [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]]
Known delays and flow control advisories [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]]

body.p: Ask for these; they are not automatic: MOA, MTR and warning area NOTAMs, airway and procedural NOTAMs, Domestic and International Notices, density altitude, and GPS RAIM availability from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]]. FDC NOTAMs for special instrument approach procedures come only on request [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1c]].

The Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) replaced the legacy Area Forecast. Static images like this Aviation Cloud Forecast show cloud coverage, bases, layers and tops with icing and mountain obscuration AIRMETs [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4b]].

callout.text: Changed: the GFA replaced the old Area Forecast (FA) for the contiguous U.S. [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4b]] [[37:10|AC 91-92 7.4.1.5]]. Area forecasts are still issued for some areas, such as Alaska and Hawaii [[34:58|AIM 7-1-1c]]. The Notices to Airmen Publication (NTAP) was discontinued June 18, 2020 [[37:11|AC 91-92 7.4.1.8.1]]. The AIM now sends you to the Domestic Notices and International Notices in the Federal NOTAM System instead [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]].

Common mistake: treating cockpit FIS-B as a full briefing. It does not carry every product or NOTAM a preflight briefing includes, and NOTAMs are limited to the past 30 days [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]]. NEXRAD can be 15 to 20 minutes old when it reaches your display [[37:13|AC 91-92 7.7]].

check.q: Departure is 3 hours away. Will a standard briefing include current conditions?
check.a: No. Current conditions are left out when departure is more than 2 hours away, unless you ask [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: plan the preflight action and fuel

bullets: 1. Departure 6 or more hours away? Get an outlook briefing for planning [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5d]].
2. Get a standard briefing (self-brief or Flight Service) as close to departure as you can, with your flight's background details [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]] [[33:323|AIM 5-1-1e]].
3. Look up runway length, surface and slope for every airport of intended use [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
4. Work takeoff and landing distances for the expected elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature. Use landing weight for landing [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]] [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]].
5. Figure trip fuel: time = distance ÷ groundspeed; fuel = time x burn. Add start, taxi and climb [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
6. Add the legal reserve (VFR 30 day or 45 night; IFR alternate plus 45), then your own margin [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]] [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].
7. Pick alternatives if the flight can't be completed: alternate airports and fuel stops [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]] [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.1]].
8. Before takeoff, get an abbreviated update if the standard briefing is 1 hour or more old [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

body.p: Worked example: day VFR, 160 NM to your first stop. Forecast winds give a 110-knot groundspeed. Cruise burn is 9 GPH.

head: Item
Work
Result
rows: Legal minimum, before taxi and climb

callout.text: Write two numbers on the plan: the legal minimum and your own minimum. Carrying enough fuel with a sufficient reserve, or planning a fuel stop, reduces the chance of a low-fuel emergency [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

check.q: Same trip, but the forecast headwind drops your groundspeed to 90 knots. New legal minimum for day VFR, before taxi and climb?

chunks.title: Risk: leaving with minimum fuel, and the familiar local flight

body.p: Fuel-related accidents are one of the top four causes of fatal general aviation accidents. Pilots still run tanks dry or starve the engine by mishandling the fuel system, planning poorly, stretching range, or not taking the time to stop for fuel [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Planning to the airplane's maximum range magnifies the hazard, and bad math, changing conditions, or not getting book speeds and burns can lead to an accident [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

**The legal minimum is a floor, not a plan.** Flying without adequate reserves usually comes from overconfidence, poor planning, or ignoring the rules [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. Always plan to be on the ground before your flight time passes what your fuel was planned for, or the gauge shows low fuel [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

RMH example: a pilot found no fuel at Knapp State (KMPV) on a weekend, estimated he had enough, and headed for White Plains as a snowstorm moved in. ATC put him in a hold, and he diverted low on fuel to Bridgeport, where the ceiling was just above minimums [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

head: If fuel gets tight in flight
What to say and what it means
rows: You can't accept any undue delay
"Minimum fuel" after your call sign. It is not an emergency and does not mean traffic priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]]
You need priority to land safely
Declare an emergency for low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]]

body.p: **The familiar local flight.** Pilots may rely on memory and familiar routes instead of procedures and checklists, and this is especially true of experienced pilots [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. RMH example: a pilot who routinely flew to one airport read a NOTAM that had moved the runway closure from 19R/1L to 19L/1R, still perceived it the old way, and started an approach to the closed runway. That is expectation bias [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

callout.text: Even for a short local hop, run the quick version: NOTAMs and TFRs, adverse conditions, current and forecast weather, runway and performance numbers, and PAVE [[37:20|AC 91-92 App B]] [[30:11|RMH 1-2]].

check.q: Approach says to expect 20 minutes of holding, and a longer delay would cut into your reserve. What do you tell ATC?
check.a: "Minimum fuel" after your call sign. It is an advisory, not an emergency. If you need priority to land safely, declare an emergency and give fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

bullets: Counting the VFR reserve from the final destination instead of the first point of intended landing [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]].
Using no-wind true airspeed for fuel time instead of forecast groundspeed [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Forgetting start, taxi and climb fuel [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Reading a POH endurance column as if it includes a reserve. Many say "no reserve" [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]].
Using sunset plus 1 hour (currency) instead of civil twilight for the night fuel reserve [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]] [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].
IFR: adding 45 minutes at the destination and forgetting the alternate leg [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]].
Skipping runway length and distance data on a "local" flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].
Using takeoff weight for the landing distance [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]].
Departing on an outlook briefing alone [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5d]].
Trusting FIS-B NOTAMs as complete [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]].
Not asking for MOA, MTR and special procedure FDC NOTAMs [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]] [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1c]].

check.q: What does "no reserve" on a POH endurance column mean for your planning?
check.a: The endurance runs the tanks dry. Take off the legal reserve, and your own, before you plan a leg [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]] [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]].

scenario.title: Dinner across the bay, home after dark
scenario.setup: You are a current commercial pilot renting a Cessna 172 you have flown for years. Saturday plan: 140 NM to a coastal airport for dinner, then home the same night. You leave at 1700, in daylight. Forecast groundspeed is 105 knots outbound and 125 knots home. Cruise burn is 8.5 GPH, and you will have 26 gallons on board. You looked at a weather app at 0800 and it "looked fine." The Chart Supplement says the destination's fuel service closes at 1900, and you expect to land about 1820. The destination runway is 2,600 ft of grass.

questions.q: Is the 0800 weather check a complete preflight action for this flight?
questions.a: No. This flight leaves the airport vicinity, so 91.103(a) requires weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives and known ATC delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]. Get a standard briefing as close to departure as you can, and an abbreviated update if it is 1 hour or more old [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]].

questions.q: What is the legal minimum fuel for the outbound leg, before taxi and climb?
questions.a: 140 ÷ 105 = 1.33 hr x 8.5 = 11.3 gal, plus 30 minutes day reserve (4.25 gal) = about 15.6 gallons [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. You have 26, so the outbound leg is legal.

questions.q: Can you skip fueling at the destination and fly home at night?
questions.a: No. You would land with about 26 - 11.3 = 14.7 gal. Home needs 140 ÷ 125 = 1.12 hr x 8.5 = 9.5 gal plus a 45-minute night reserve (6.4 gal) = 15.9 gal [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. Get fuel before 1900, or plan a fuel stop. The RMH KMPV story shows how "I think it's enough" goes wrong [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

questions.q: What runway information must you have for the grass field?
questions.a: Its runway length and your takeoff and landing distance data for the expected elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. On the PHAK sample chart a dry grass runway adds 15% of the ground roll for takeoff [[1:278|PHAK Figure 11-24]], and the landing sample adds 20% of the total to clear 50 ft [[1:283|PHAK Figure 11-32]]. Use your own POH's correction.

questions.q: The briefing shows a NOTAM: your home airport's runway lights are out of service tonight. You have landed there hundreds of times. What now?
questions.a: Treat it as new information, not the usual. Expectation bias makes familiar pilots read NOTAMs the way things used to be [[30:45|RMH 6-2]]. Plan an alternative if the planned flight can't be completed, such as a lighted airport nearby, and refigure the fuel for it [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].

skills.do: For a flight the reviewer gives you, list the 91.103 items that apply, get and summarize a standard briefing, show runway length and takeoff and landing distances for each airport, and work the legal minimum fuel and your own planned fuel for day VFR, night VFR or IFR.
skills.practice: Plan a real trip using AC 91-92 Appendix B as your checklist [[37:20|AC 91-92 App B]]. Work the PHAK takeoff and landing samples, then repeat them with your own POH [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]] [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]]. Show the fuel math with the 91.151 or 91.167 reserve written out [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]].

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.3, who is the final authority as to the operation of the aircraft?
options: The air traffic controller
The pilot in command
The aircraft owner
The operator's chief pilot
quiz.why: The PIC is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]].

quiz.q: You deviated from a Part 91 rule to handle an in-flight emergency. When must you send a written report?
options: Within 10 days of the deviation, in every case
Only if the Administrator requests it
Within 48 hours of landing, in every case
Only if the airplane was damaged or someone was hurt
quiz.why: 91.3(c) requires the report only on the Administrator's request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]]. The 48-hour report in 91.123(d) is for ATC priority, and only if ATC asks [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

quiz.q: Which 91.103 item applies to every flight, even a trip around the pattern?
options: Any known traffic delays of which ATC has advised you
Alternatives available if the planned flight cannot be completed
Runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data
Weather reports and forecasts for the departure airport
quiz.why: 91.103(b) applies to any flight. The other items are named in (a), for IFR flights and flights not in the vicinity of an airport [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

quiz.q: Day VFR in an airplane. How much fuel must be left after reaching the first point of intended landing, at normal cruise?
options: 20 minutes
45 minutes
30 minutes
60 minutes
quiz.why: Day: at least 30 minutes; night: 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]. 20 minutes is the rotorcraft rule.

quiz.q: For the 91.151 night fuel reserve, night begins:
options: At official sunset, as published in the Air Almanac
1 hour after sunset, as used for passenger-carrying currency
At 2100 local time, whatever the season or latitude
At the end of evening civil twilight
quiz.why: 14 CFR 1.1 defines night as the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. Sunset plus 1 hour is the 61.57(b) currency period [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

quiz.q: IFR with an alternate required. The 45-minute reserve is counted from:
options: Takeoff
Arrival at the destination
Top of descent
Arrival at the alternate
quiz.why: 91.167(a) requires fuel to the destination, then to the alternate, then 45 minutes at normal cruise [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]].

quiz.q: The destination has an instrument approach. Which forecast lets you leave out the alternate fuel under 91.167(b)?
options: At the ETA only: ceiling 1,000 ft, visibility 3 SM
1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA: ceiling 2,000 ft, visibility 3 SM
1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA: ceiling 3,000 ft, visibility 2 SM
2 hours before to 2 hours after ETA: ceiling 2,000 ft, visibility 2 SM
quiz.why: For airplanes: at least 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, ceiling at least 2,000 ft above airport elevation and visibility at least 3 SM [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]].

quiz.q: Cockpit NEXRAD weather is on your display. How old can that radar picture be by the time it appears?
options: Up to 15 to 20 minutes old
Under 1 minute old, effectively live
Up to 2 hours old
Up to 30 days old, like FIS-B NOTAMs
quiz.why: NEXRAD is a mosaic of data sets that can be 15 to 20 minutes old by the time it is assembled and displayed, which can make it harder to correlate and apply [[37:13|AC 91-92 7.7]]. The 30 day limit applies to FIS-B NOTAMs only [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]].

quiz.q: You tell ATC "minimum fuel." What does that mean?
options: You are declaring a fuel emergency and requesting priority handling
You have less than 30 minutes of usable fuel remaining at cruise
ATC must give you traffic priority ahead of other arrivals
You can't accept undue delay, but it is not an emergency
quiz.why: Minimum fuel is an advisory that an emergency is possible with undue delay. It is not an emergency and does not imply priority [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

takeaways: The PIC is the final authority and owns the go or no-go decision (91.3).
91.103(b) applies to every flight: runway lengths and takeoff and landing data, even for a local hop.
VFR airplane: fuel to the first stop plus 30 minutes day or 45 minutes night (civil twilight), at normal cruise.
IFR: destination plus alternate (unless 1-2-3) plus 45 minutes at normal cruise.
A self-briefing can be compliant. Standard close to departure, abbreviated to update, outlook when 6+ hours out.
The legal minimum is a floor. Plan your own reserve and a fuel stop.
Familiar flight? Still read the NOTAMs. Expectation bias catches experienced pilots.
cfi_notes: PHAK 13-5 still says the briefing should come from an FSS specialist. Teach the current AIM 5-1-1a and 7-1-5a line: a regulatory compliant briefing does not require contacting Flight Service. The same PHAK page also still mentions the "NOTAM publication" (NTAP), which AC 91-92 says was discontinued June 18, 2020.
Probe 91.103(a) versus (b). Many experienced pilots believe a local flight needs nothing. Ask which items are required for a pattern flight and why.
Ask "night by which definition?" The 91.151 reserve uses 14 CFR 1.1 civil twilight; 61.57(b) currency uses sunset plus 1 hour to sunrise minus 1 hour. Reviewers often catch this mix-up.
Ask "counted from where?" VFR reserve from the first point of intended landing; IFR 45 minutes after the alternate when one is required.

AC 91-92 is not fully consistent: 7.2.3 and the AIM say outlook for 6 or more hours, Appendix B.1 says more than 6 hours, and Table 1 says 6 to 48 hours. Appendix B.3 says abbreviated updates up to 2 hours before flight, while 8.1 says get one if the standard is 1 hour or more old. Teach the AIM wording.
Have the pilot work their own POH takeoff, landing and cruise charts during the review. Point out "no reserve" on endurance columns and the landing weight versus takeoff weight trap.
Use the two RMH 6-2 stories (KMPV with no fuel; the NOTAM read the old way) to open R1 and R2. Ask what they would have done differently at the planning table.
gaps: No source gives a recommended personal fuel reserve above the 91.151 and 91.167 minimums; personal reserves are set by the pilot, ideally with an instructor.
The Chart Supplement legend (codes for elevation, fuel, lighting and runway weight bearing) is not among the sources; pilots should use the legend in the Chart Supplement itself.
Actual takeoff, landing, climb and cruise numbers come from each airplane's POH or AFM; the PHAK charts are samples only.

No source gives a takeoff or landing safety factor for small airplanes. AC 91-79B's dispatch landing-distance planning is required for large transport airplanes under Parts 91K, 121 and 135 and only recommended for other Part 91 operators [[27:10|AC 91-79B 2.1.1]].
Third-party flight planning apps and their briefing formats are not covered; AC 91-92 only says to know their accuracy disclaimers [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.1]].

activities.title: 91.103: every flight, or IFR and away from the airport?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: IFR or away from an airport: 91.103(a)

items.t: Runway lengths at airports of intended use
Landing distance for expected weight, wind and temperature
Alternatives if the planned flight can't be completed
Known traffic delays ATC has advised you of

activities.title: Read the takeoff chart
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Total to clear 50 ft: 2,400 lb, 3,000 ft, 30 °C

activities.title: Minimum legal fuel
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer. Ignore taxi and climb fuel.

items.q: Day VFR in an airplane. 1 hour 45 minutes to your first stop with forecast winds, 8 GPH at normal cruise. Least fuel to begin the flight?
items.why: 1.75 hr + 0.5 hr day reserve = 2.25 hr x 8 GPH = 18.0 gallons [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]].

items.q: Night VFR. 2 hours 10 minutes to your first stop, 9.5 GPH. Least fuel to begin the flight?
items.why: 2.17 hr + 0.75 hr night reserve = 2.92 hr x 9.5 GPH = 27.7 gallons [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]].

items.q: PHAK cruise table: 5,000 ft at 2,400 rpm shows 38 gallons gives 5.5 hours endurance, no reserve. Day VFR: longest flight time to your first stop you may plan?
items.why: Endurance 5.5 hr has no reserve [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. Subtract the 30-minute day reserve: 5.5 - 0.5 = 5.0 hours [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]].

items.q: IFR. 1 hour 20 minutes to destination, 30 minutes from there to the alternate, 10 GPH. Minimum fuel?
IFR to an airport with an ILS. Forecast from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA: 3,000 ft broken, 6 SM. 2 hours 30 minutes en route, 12 GPH. Minimum fuel?

activities.title: Briefing types and terms
activities.intro: Tap a briefing term, then what it means.

pairs.r: Departure 6 or more hours away; planning only
No earlier briefing; the complete picture
Updates an earlier briefing or gives one or two items
Your own review with online tools; may be compliant
Briefer's advisory; the go or no-go call is yours
A briefing or update by radio from Flight Service

activities.title: True or false: what the briefing gives you
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A standard briefing includes current conditions even when departure is 4 hours away.
cards.why: False. Current conditions are left out when departure is more than 2 hours away, unless you ask [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]].

cards.s: Winds aloft from a Flight Service briefer are referenced to true north.
cards.why: True. Winds aloft are given in knots and degrees, referenced to true north [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]].

cards.s: FIS-B in the cockpit carries every NOTAM a full preflight briefing would.
cards.why: False. FIS-B may not include all products or NOTAMs, and NOTAMs are limited to the past 30 days [[37:14|AC 91-92 7.7]].

cards.s: "VFR flight not recommended" is advisory; the final decision is the pilot's.
cards.why: True. The final decision as to whether the flight can be made safely rests solely with the pilot [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]].

cards.s: Briefers give FDC NOTAMs for special instrument approach procedures automatically.
cards.why: False. Pilots authorized to use them must specifically ask [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1c]].

cards.s: The destination forecast covers significant changes from 1 hour before to 1 hour after your ETA.

activities.title: Can I legally and safely make this trip?
activities.intro: You are flying N4521K, a rental Cessna 172 you know well, on a Friday: 120 NM to a coastal airport, then home. You plan to leave at 1800 in daylight and fly home around 2100, after the end of civil twilight. 30 gallons on board, 9 GPH at cruise.

steps.s: At 1630 you open your flight planning app. You last looked at the weather at 0700. What do you do?
options: Nothing more; the morning look counts
Get a standard briefing for the whole round trip now
Check only the destination TAF
Ask for an outlook briefing
steps.why: Get a standard briefing as close to departure as possible [[37:14|AC 91-92 8.1]]. An outlook briefing is for departures 6 or more hours away [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5d]]. A self-brief can be compliant [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1a]].

steps.s: Forecast headwinds give 100 knots groundspeed outbound. What is the legal minimum fuel to begin the outbound leg, before taxi and climb?
options: 15.3 gallons
12.3 gallons
10.8 gallons
17.6 gallons
steps.why: 120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 hr x 9 = 10.8 gal, plus 30 minutes day reserve (4.5 gal) = 15.3 gallons [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. 10.8 has no reserve.

steps.s: The Chart Supplement says the destination FBO closes at 1900. You land at 1915. Home is at night with a 130-knot groundspeed. About 19 gallons remain. Fuel there?
options: Skip it; the fuel gauges will warn you well before the tanks run low, so no call is needed
Skip it; only a 30-minute reserve is needed, so about 19 gallons is far more than enough
It is illegal; night VFR needs a 60-minute reserve, so you must find fuel before leaving
Legal on paper (about 19 on board, about 15 needed), but call ahead for fuel and pick a backup stop
steps.why: Home: 120 ÷ 130 = 0.92 hr x 9 = 8.3 gal plus the 45-minute night reserve (6.75 gal) = about 15.1 gal [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. That margin is thin once you count taxi and climb. Planning a fuel stop reduces low-fuel risk [[30:39|RMH 5-1]], and the KMPV story shows what happens when the fuel isn't there [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

steps.s: Your briefing lists a NOTAM: your home airport's runway lights are out of service from 2030 tonight. You have landed there hundreds of times.
options: Land anyway at your home field, since you know it well and have landed there many times
Ignore it, because lighting NOTAMs are routine and the lights are usually back on soon
Plan to a lighted airport nearby and refigure fuel for it
Plan to ask the tower to turn the runway lights on when you arrive after 2030
steps.why: 91.103(a) asks for alternatives if the planned flight can't be completed [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]. Familiar pilots tend to read NOTAMs the old way, which is expectation bias [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

steps.s: Heading to the lighted airport, a stronger headwind means you'll land with about 35 minutes of fuel. Approach says expect a 10-minute delay.
options: Advise "minimum fuel," and divert closer if more delay builds
Accept the delay quietly, since you were legal on fuel at takeoff and still have 35 minutes
Stay quiet, because a minimum fuel advisory automatically requires priority handling from ATC
Declare an emergency at once and demand a straight-in ahead of all other traffic
steps.why: Say "minimum fuel" when you can't accept undue delay; it is not an emergency. If you need priority, declare an emergency and give fuel in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]]. Plan to be on the ground before the gauge shows low fuel [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

final_quiz.q: You will fly a 50 NM VFR cross-country to a friend's airport. Under 91.103, what must your preflight action include at a minimum?
options: Weather, fuel, alternatives and known ATC delays, plus runway lengths and takeoff and landing data
Only runway lengths and takeoff and landing distance data, because the flight is VFR and not under IFR
Only weather reports, forecasts and NOTAMs for the route, since the flight is VFR and fairly short
Only the items a Flight Service standard briefing provides, such as weather, NOTAMs and winds aloft
final_quiz.why: A flight not in the vicinity of an airport needs the 91.103(a) items, and every flight needs the (b) items [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

final_quiz.q: Day VFR: 2 hours 15 minutes to your first stop with forecast winds, 10 GPH at normal cruise. Ignoring taxi and climb, what is the least fuel you may begin with?
options: 22.5 gallons
25.0 gallons
30.0 gallons
27.5 gallons
final_quiz.why: (2.25 + 0.5) hr x 10 = 27.5 gallons [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. 22.5 has no reserve; 30.0 uses the night reserve.

final_quiz.q: A night VFR flight leaves at 2030, well after the end of civil twilight. It is 1 hour 40 minutes to your first stop at 9 GPH. Least fuel, ignoring taxi and climb?
options: About 21.8 gallons
About 19.5 gallons
About 15.0 gallons
About 24.0 gallons
final_quiz.why: (1.67 + 0.75) hr x 9 = about 21.8 gallons [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. 19.5 uses the day reserve; 24.0 uses a full hour.

final_quiz.q: IFR to an airport forecast 1,200 overcast and 4 SM at your ETA. 1 hour 30 minutes to destination, 40 minutes to the alternate, 11 GPH. Minimum fuel under 91.167?
options: About 32.1 gallons
About 24.8 gallons
About 29.3 gallons
About 23.8 gallons
final_quiz.why: A 1,200 ft ceiling fails the 2,000 ft test, so the alternate leg counts [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]]. 1.5 + 0.67 + 0.75 = 2.92 hr x 11 = about 32.1 gallons [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]].

final_quiz.q: IFR to an airport with an ILS. The TAF shows 2,500 broken and 5 SM from 1 hour before to 1 hour after your ETA. What fuel does 91.167 require?
options: To the destination and the alternate, plus 30 minutes
To the destination and the alternate, plus 45 minutes
To the destination, plus 30 minutes at normal cruise
To the destination, plus 45 minutes at normal cruise
final_quiz.why: The approach and the 1-2-3 forecast remove the alternate leg [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]], leaving destination plus 45 minutes [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]].

final_quiz.q: PHAK short-field chart: 2,400 lb, 3,000 ft pressure altitude, 30 °C, 9-knot headwind. What total distance do you need to clear a 50 ft obstacle?
options: About 1,984 ft
About 2,480 ft
About 2,232 ft
About 1,193 ft
final_quiz.why: The chart gives 2,480 ft; subtract 10% for 9 knots of headwind: 2,480 - 248 = 2,232 ft [[1:278|PHAK Figure 11-24]]. 1,984 is the 18-knot answer [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]].

final_quiz.q: PHAK landing table: 2,500 ft and 50 °F, 8-knot headwind. Total landing distance to clear a 50 ft obstacle?
options: About 376 ft
About 1,022 ft
About 1,135 ft
About 908 ft
final_quiz.why: 1,135 ft minus 10% per 4 knots of headwind (20%) = 908 ft [[1:283|PHAK Figure 11-32]]. 376 ft is the reduced ground roll.

final_quiz.q: The Chart Supplement shows your landing runway slopes 1.0% down in your landing direction. Compared with the level-runway chart number, expect:
options: A longer landing roll
A shorter landing roll
No change; slope affects only takeoff
No change if the runway is grooved
final_quiz.why: Landing on a downsloping runway increases landing distance [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

final_quiz.q: You self-briefed in an app at 1200 and call Flight Service at 1300 for a 1400 departure. What should you ask for?
options: A standard briefing, without mentioning that you already self-briefed in an app earlier
An abbreviated briefing, saying when and where you got your earlier information
An outlook briefing, since the departure is only an hour away and the weather looks stable
NOTAMs only, since the app already covered the weather and everything else you need
final_quiz.why: An abbreviated briefing updates earlier information; tell the briefer the time and source of what you have [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5c]] [[33:323|AIM 5-1-1f]].

final_quiz.q: During a standard phone briefing, which of these must you specifically ask for?
options: Adverse conditions
GPS RAIM availability
The destination forecast
Winds aloft
final_quiz.why: RAIM availability is an upon-request item [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5b]]. The others are given automatically in a standard briefing [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5b]].

final_quiz.q: You fly from your home field almost daily. A NOTAM now closes the other parallel runway than the one closed last month. What hazard does the RMH tie to this?
options: Hypoxia: the pilot's thinking dulled by too little oxygen
Get-there-itis: pressing on to land despite a known closure
Expectation bias: reading the NOTAM the way it used to be
Resignation: giving up and accepting a bad situation as unavoidable
final_quiz.why: In the RMH example a pilot read the changed NOTAM the old way and approached the closed runway: expectation bias [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH cruise table shows 5.5 hours endurance with no reserve at your power setting. For a night VFR leg, what is the longest flight time to your first stop you may plan, ignoring taxi and climb?
options: 5 hours 30 minutes
5 hours
4 hours 45 minutes
4 hours 30 minutes
final_quiz.why: No reserve means the tanks run dry at 5.5 hours [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. Subtract the 45-minute night reserve: 4 hours 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Must you call Flight Service to meet 91.103?
options: No; a self-briefing may be compliant
Yes for IFR flights, no for VFR
Only for flights over 50 NM
Yes; only Flight Service briefings count
final_quiz.why: Pilots can receive a regulatory compliant briefing without contacting Flight Service [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1a]] [[37:7|AC 91-92 7.1]].

final_quiz.q: A friend says a local VFR flight that stays near the airport needs no preflight action. What does 91.103 actually require?
options: Nothing for a local flight, since the weather and fuel items apply only to IFR flights
Only a NOTAM check for the airport, since the other items apply to cross-country flights
Runway lengths and distance data, plus all available information about the flight
A standard briefing from Flight Service, which is required before every flight including local ones
final_quiz.why: The opening sentence covers all available information, and 91.103(b) applies to any flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].
